title: II Samuel: A New Translation with Introduction, Notes, and Commentary (The Anchor Bible, vol. 9)
author: P. Kyle McCarter Jr.
allowedUseNotes: Modern copyrighted critical commentary. Project stores only its own summary/paraphrase of McCarter's discussion, with a single short attributed quotation (under 15 words) of his own stated conclusion; no reproduction of his translation, textual notes, or broader commentary.
summary: McCarter's Anchor Bible commentary on 2 Samuel, a standard modern critical reference for the book. On 2 Samuel 1:1-16, McCarter notes the episode's structural resemblance to the messenger scene at 1 Samuel 4:12-17 (the fugitive who brings news of a battlefield disaster) and treats the Amalekite's claim to have killed Saul as fundamentally unresolved by the narrative itself: commenting on whether David was taken in by the messenger's story, McCarter writes that '[w]hether David was deceived or not, we cannot tell' (McCarter, II Samuel, p. 63). This project cites McCarter for that narrower, agnostic point — that a leading modern critical commentary treats the reliability question as genuinely open in the text rather than as a settled harmonization problem — rather than for adopting either of the two more specific scholarlyViews (outright fabrication vs. looter's embellishment of a genuine find) surfaced from the two public-domain commentaries also cited on this claim (Keil & Delitzsch 1866; Gill's Exposition 1748-63). Queue #20a researcher pass (2026-08-12) extended this card's coverage to 2 Samuel 3-4, the chapters covering Abner's break with Ish-bosheth, his death, and Ish-bosheth's assassination. McCarter is the originator of the 'apology of David' reading applied throughout this stretch of text (first argued in his own 1980 Journal of Biblical Literature article, cited on this project as its own card, mccarter-1980-apology-of-david, since it long predates and stands independently of this 1984 commentary) — the thesis that 1-2 Samuel's narration of the convenient deaths of Saul, Abner, and Ish-bosheth is shaped throughout to defend David against real contemporary accusations of having orchestrated them. This project's claim-public-response cites McCarter (via mccarter-1980-apology-of-david) directly for that reading as applied to 2 Samuel 3:36-37's insistence that 'it had not been the king's will to put Abner to death.' A specific, page-verified McCarter comment on the political meaning of Abner's going in to Rizpah (3:6-11, claim-abner-break) or on the 2 Samuel 4:6 MT/LXX textual crux (claim-ish-bosheth-assassination) specifically was searched for but not found via secondary corroboration in this pass, despite McCarter's Anchor Bible commentaries being well documented (via multiple independent secondary sources) as containing systematic verse-by-verse Textual Notes sections that regularly weigh the Old Greek/Qumran witnesses against the Masoretic Text for exactly this kind of crux in Samuel — see this card's confidenceNotes. Queue #22 researcher pass (2026-08-24) extended coverage to 2 Samuel 5, the united-kingdom covenant, the capture of Jerusalem, the Hiram building notice, and the two Rephaim Valley engagements. McCarter's Anchor Bible commentary is a standard critical-commentary venue for the position that tsinnor's precise meaning in 5:8 cannot be recovered with confidence (the third scholarlyView on claim-tsinnor-crux); a specific, page-verified McCarter statement on the word itself was searched for but not found via secondary corroboration this pass (the same 'checked, permanently thin for this specific point' outcome as the 4:6 crux above) — this card is cited on that scholarlyView as representative of the broader critical-commentary position, not as a page-verified direct quotation. McCarter is also cited generally on claim-philistine-reaction and the two Rephaim-engagement claims (the topical-vs-chronological arrangement question at 5:17, and the MT/LXX and Geba/Gibeon textual variants at 5:21 and 5:25) as the standard modern critical-commentary venue for exactly this kind of text-critical and compositional question in Samuel, consistent with how it is already used for 2 Samuel 3-4.
